source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)

coverage.syllabus: Lubbers Fall 2026 §9.4: factual issues in informal actions, Baltimore Gas and Electric, FCC Prometheus, census pretext case, OSHA EtO Problem 9, pp. 658–668

topics.title: § 9.4 — Review of Facts in Informal Proceedings (pp. 658–663)
topics.description: Factual component of APA §706(2)(A), substantial evidence §706(2)(E), Data Processing, predictive science and FCC Prometheus.

entries.title: Informal agency factfinding reviewed as arbitrary/capricious
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Informal action lacks §706(2)(E) formal record gateway but agency's factual premises still reviewed for reasonableness under §706(2)(A).
entries.laymanExplanation: An informal safety rule must still have plausible evidence behind its facts.
entries.legalExplanation: Courts expanded §706(2)(A) to test factual bases as informal rulemaking gained large consequences.
entries.examApplication: First determine if formal on-the-record hearing or §553 informal procedure; then identify fact vs discretion.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume factual assertions in informal action are beyond review.

entries.title: Data Processing: factual review standards often largely semantic
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Scalia's Data Processing decision said factual sufficiency under substantial evidence and arbitrary/capricious may be similar, but formal proceedings provide a different record and hearing process.
entries.laymanExplanation: Both standards ask whether facts reasonably support what agency concluded.
entries.legalExplanation: D.C. Circuit observed federal appellate consensus; Supreme Court Dickinson v Zurko acknowledged without firmly adopting.
entries.examApplication: Explain why congressionally prescribed OSHA substantial evidence still warrants separate mention.
entries.examTrap: Not universally identical for every federal statute and review issue.

entries.title: Association of Data Processing Service Organizations v. Federal Reserve, 745 F.2d 677
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: D.C. Circuit described factual reasonableness equivalence between §706(2)(E) and factual part §706(2)(A).
entries.laymanExplanation: Label matters less than supporting evidence.
entries.legalExplanation: Formal record requirements remain meaningful.
entries.examApplication: Compare OSHA rulemaking and ordinary EPA notice-comment.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook Notes, not full opinion excerpt

entries.title: OSH Act §655(f) substantial evidence standard
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: OSHA worker safety standards must be supported by substantial evidence considering whole record; circuit views differ whether that is more rigorous than factual arbitrariness.
entries.laymanExplanation: OSHA needs substantial scientific support, not certainty.
entries.legalExplanation: Evaluate significant-risk threshold, scientific data and agency explanation separately.
entries.examApplication: Use statutory standard specifically in EtO analysis.
entries.examTrap: The statute does not impose a criminal burden of proof.

entries.title: Baltimore Gas: greatest deference at frontiers of science
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Courts generally most deferential when technical agency predicts uncertain scientific impacts, e.g., NRC assessment of long-term nuclear waste.
entries.laymanExplanation: An expert agency can make uncertain forecasts if it explains how.
entries.legalExplanation: Baltimore Gas & Electric upheld nuclear waste model, contrasting State Farm's ignored evidence/alternatives.
entries.examApplication: When applying to EtO, examine limitations of studies and reason for extrapolation.
entries.examTrap: Science deference is not immunity for irrational speculation.

entries.title: Baltimore Gas & Electric Co. v. NRDC, 462 U.S. 87 (1983)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court upheld NRC predictive nuclear-waste impacts model within technical expertise.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judges allow reasonable expert estimates at scientific frontier.
entries.legalExplanation: Only case discussion, not full opinion reproduced.
entries.examApplication: Contrast State Farm's missing explanation.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook Notes, not full opinion excerpt

entries.title: FCC Prometheus: zone of reasonableness and no mandatory independent study
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: FCC predicted ownership-rule repeal unlikely to reduce minority/female-owned broadcasting with imperfect available evidence; APA doesn't impose universal duty to commission statistics.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency may make reasonable forecast without perfect research.
entries.legalExplanation: Comments had no forward-looking statistical proof despite FCC invitations; Supreme Court upheld rational prediction.
entries.examApplication: Identify evidence actually available and why agency inference reasonable.

entries.title: FCC v. Prometheus Radio Project, 592 U.S. 414 (2021)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court unanimously upheld FCC media ownership predictive judgment; reversed demand for better empirical study.
entries.laymanExplanation: Reasonable prediction can survive with imperfect data.
entries.legalExplanation: Kavanaugh described agency's 'zone of reasonableness'.
entries.examApplication: Compare quality and relevance of opposing studies.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook Notes, not full opinion excerpt

entries.title: Predictive judgment must still connect facts to choice
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Uncertainty may be resolved through informed expertise but agency cannot merely recite 'uncertain'; should address known contradictory or useful data.
entries.laymanExplanation: Scientists can extrapolate, but explain methods and limits.
entries.legalExplanation: State Farm and NRDC v Herrington constrain needless uncertain assumptions.
entries.examApplication: Describe data, inference, alternatives and unresolved uncertainty.
entries.examTrap: A mere 'science is complex' sentence will not do.

entries.title: Colorado state judgmental facts and liquor license standards
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court upheld rules controlling sexually oriented activities in liquor-licensed venues with police testimony/experience about crime despite no definitive quantitative proof.
entries.laymanExplanation: Expert practical law-enforcement experience may inform prospective policy.
entries.legalExplanation: Citizens for Free Enterprise v Department of Revenue applied Colorado record law and acknowledged substantial policy component.
entries.examApplication: State experience-based data may be enough; explain relevance.

topics.title: § 9.4 — Administrative Record, Pretext and State Approaches (pp. 663–667)
topics.description: Closed-record review, narrowly permitted supplements, Census citizenship question pretext, open vs closed state review.

entries.title: Federal default: closed record as it existed at agency decision
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court reviews materials before agency at decision time, even in informal proceedings; additional court-developed evidence generally excluded.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judge sees the record agency had, not new expert reports made later.
entries.legalExplanation: Overton Park, Camp v Pitts and IMS v Alvarez ground existing-record principle; notice-comment need not use formal hearing to have a reviewable record.
entries.examApplication: Compare existing agency docs and later challenges; check record completeness.
entries.examTrap: Court does not retry every scientific dispute from scratch.

entries.title: Four narrow extra-record exceptions (Lands Council)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Extra-record material may be allowed to test failure to consider relevant factors or explain action, recover documents agency relied on but omitted, clarify complex scientific terms, or prove bad faith.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can sometimes look outside file if agency hid documents, experts need to explain a term, or officials lied.
entries.legalExplanation: Lands Council said exceptions narrowly construed; distinguish completion of record from entirely new merits evidence.
entries.examApplication: Specify exact legal exception and supporting evidentiary showing.
entries.examTrap: New competing study from plaintiff alone generally insufficient.

entries.title: Lands Council v. Regional Forester, 395 F.3d 1019 (9th Cir. 2005)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Textbook lists four narrow extra-record reasons under this precedent.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rare exceptions to closed review.
entries.legalExplanation: Not a license for full court trial.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook Notes, not full opinion excerpt

entries.title: Strong showing of bad faith allows pretext scrutiny
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency's asserted rationale must be genuine; rare contradiction between decision history and sole stated justification may warrant unusual record discovery.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government can have political preferences, but shouldn't invent a fake legal explanation.
entries.legalExplanation: Overton Park 'strong showing', Department of Commerce census case illustrated staged effort to solicit DOJ request after desired decision set.
entries.examApplication: Build chronology: what agency wanted, who requested, stated explanation and contrary records.
entries.examTrap: Mixed motives alone do not prove pretext.

entries.title: Department of Commerce v. New York, 588 U.S. 752 (2019) — Census citizenship question
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Ross cited DOJ Voting Rights Act enforcement for citizenship question; evidence revealed desire predated request and DOJ justification was solicited. Supreme Court held stated reason contrived; Thomas dissent warned discovery fishing expeditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency's explanation cannot be staged cover story.
entries.legalExplanation: Roberts majority distinguished sole fake reason from ordinary additional political motives.
entries.examApplication: Contrast majority's record contradiction with Thomas regularity concerns.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook Notes, not full opinion excerpt

entries.title: Thomas dissent in Census pretext case
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Dissent warned expanded pretext theory allows politically motivated discovery, depositions and obstruction of routine policymaking.
entries.laymanExplanation: Too much probing into motives can turn every policy dispute into a trial of officials.
entries.legalExplanation: Important balance to strong-showing standard.
entries.examApplication: Present critical perspective without claiming majority adopted it.

entries.title: States may use open record in informal adjudication
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Some states permit evidence beyond agency file for informal or ministerial action; federal practice generally closed.
entries.laymanExplanation: If agency had no reliable file, state court may consider extra facts.
entries.legalExplanation: Lake Sunapee and Western States contrast state approaches.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish formal adjudication, informal administrative choice and rulemaking.
entries.examTrap: Federal record rule not automatically state rule.

entries.title: State rulemaking: closed record prevents sandbagging/de novo policymaking
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Many states, including California for rulemaking, limit new expert proof to protect administrative primacy and avoid post hoc judicial science trials.
entries.laymanExplanation: If objector held back evidence until court, judges might become policymakers.
entries.legalExplanation: Western States Petroleum explains cost, finality and institutional concerns; counterargument fairness to absent participants.
entries.examApplication: Assess state statute and equity of participation.
entries.examTrap: Closed record doesn't automatically bar narrow evidence of bad faith.

entries.title: Western States Petroleum Association v. Superior Court, 888 P.2d 1268 (Cal. 1995)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: California declined open-record rulemaking challenge because new competing scientists could turn judicial review into de novo test of wisdom.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency, not judge, makes quasi-legislative technical policy.
entries.legalExplanation: Discusses preserving finality and reducing sandbagging.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish state ministerial action.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in textbook Notes, not full opinion excerpt

topics.title: § 9.4 — OSHA Ethylene Oxide (EtO) Exposure & STEL — Assigned Problem (pp. 667–668)
topics.description: OSHA significant-risk Benzene, feasibility Cotton Dust, EtO science, occupational substantial evidence, short-term exposure alternative.

entries.title: OSHA health protection threshold: significant risk and feasibility
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: OSHA must first find significant workplace risk (Benzene) then protect against material health impairment to extent technologically/economically feasible (Cotton Dust), subject to substantial evidence §655(f).
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency must protect workers as fully as feasible once significant hazard shown; it needn't maximize simple net-dollar benefits.
entries.legalExplanation: Cost-effectiveness alone not substitute for statutory feasibility; uncertainties in toxicology require reasoned extrapolation.
entries.examApplication: Separately analyze significant risk, 1 ppm feasible limit, evidence, reasoned rejection of STEL.
entries.examTrap: Lower-cost 5 ppm alternative is not automatically mandated by executive CBA.

entries.title: EtO empirical record: three distinct study limitations
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Hogstedt leukemia: 3 deaths vs 0.2 expected in 230 exposed workers. Bushy Run rats: cancers after 100ppm/60ppm exposure but viral illness. Hemminki nurses: greater reported miscarriages with purpose-awareness questionnaire bias.
entries.laymanExplanation: Evidence points to danger but every study has a possible weakness.
entries.legalExplanation: Scientific extrapolation and confounding do not prove facts false, but agency should explain why evidence collectively supports standard.
entries.examApplication: Quantify 3/0.2 = 15 times expected (do not treat as precise causal risk ratio); explain viral confound and survey bias.
entries.examTrap: Statistical association and precise human dose response are separate.

entries.title: EtO quantitative facts provided in problem
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Prior 50 ppm eight-hour average replaced with 1 ppm; 5 ppm would save 85% of compliance cost; zero exposure not feasible; OSHA projected 12–23 excess cancer deaths even at 1 ppm.
entries.laymanExplanation: The new average maximum is 1/50 prior limit, but still not zero risk.
entries.legalExplanation: Use as factual inputs for qualitative review; rat-to-human models require assumptions.
entries.examApplication: Compute 50 to 1 is 98% lower numerical limit; compare savings and residual risks without predetermining legal choice.

entries.title: Proposed 10 ppm short-term exposure limit not adopted
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: OSHA initially proposed no brief peak over 10 ppm (STEL) but decided 1 ppm full-shift average would suffice, after OMB complained of expense and inadequate benefits.
entries.laymanExplanation: A low average might still allow high spike; agency must explain why added peak limit unnecessary.
entries.legalExplanation: Separate short-term and long-term exposure risks; §706 reasoned decision and statute protect workers where feasible.
entries.examApplication: Ask if agency had studies of peak exposures and causal injury; what did OMB say and what OSHA actually relied on?
entries.examTrap: OMB policy cost objections cannot displace statute's health-protection command.

problems.title: Substantial evidence vs arbitrary factual review
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 658–660)
problems.prompt: Compare formal §706(2)(E) and informal §706(2)(A) with Data Processing. Does OSHA §655(f) change outcome or only label?

problems.title: State Farm versus Baltimore Gas and Prometheus
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 660–662)
problems.prompt: Differentiate rational scientific projection with incomplete data from unexplained rejection of obvious safety alternative and unsupported uncertainty.

problems.title: Predictive facts from police expertise
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 662–663)
problems.prompt: Can state agency rely on experienced police testimony to justify rule without controlled empirical crime studies? Evaluate state record review.

problems.title: Closed record and concealed expert material
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 663–664)
problems.prompt: Compare newly commissioned anti-agency expert testimony and preexisting technical memorandum agency secretly relied on. When does Lands Council permit supplement?

problems.title: Census pretext evidence
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 664–666)
problems.prompt: Agency initiated decision before requesting DOJ VRA rationale. Is this contrived official explanation or permissible mixed motives? Consider Roberts and Thomas.

problems.title: States and sandbagging
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 666–667)
problems.prompt: Should a court accept new data to challenge rule where person did not comment? Compare California closed record and more permissive state informal decisions.

problems.title: OSHA EtO 1 ppm and 10 ppm STEL — professor-assigned problem
problems.kind: Textbook Problem 9 / Professor-assigned group presentation — UNSOLVED
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 667–668)
problems.prompt: OSHA replaced 50 ppm workday average limit with 1 ppm, relying on Hogstedt 3 leukemia deaths vs 0.2 expected (230 exposed), Bushy Run cancer in high-dose rats with viral illness and Hemminki nurses reporting miscarriages with survey bias. 1 ppm based on rat/human mathematical assumptions, leaves 12–23 excess cancer deaths; 5 ppm would save hospitals 85% compliance cost but zero infeasible. OMB objected to proposed 10 ppm short-term STEL; OSHA omitted STEL saying full-day cap enough. Industry challenges 1 ppm; public-interest challengers attack absent STEL. Apply (a) Benzene significant risk, (b) Cotton Dust technological/economic feasibility versus pure CBA, (c) OSHA §655(f) substantial evidence and predictive-science deference, (d) State Farm relevant factors and STEL alternative, separately. Leave merits unresolved.

problems.title: EtO numerical and bias drill
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 667–668)
problems.prompt: Compute observed/expected Hogstedt leukemia ratio and percentage decline 50 to 1 ppm; note why those arithmetic facts do not settle causation, feasibility or standard of review.

problems.title: EtO average versus peak exposure
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 9, pp. 658–668 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 668)
problems.prompt: Does 1 ppm averaged over eight hours rule out high short-term peaks? What must OSHA explain about 10 ppm STEL when rejecting proposed separate limit?
